claim: Natural killer (NK) cells recognize target cells through germline-encoded activation and inhibitory receptors enabling effective immunity against viruses and cancer.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells recognize target cells through germline-encoded activation and inhibitory receptors enabling effective immunity against viruses and cancer.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on NK cell function

claim: The Ly49 receptor family in the mouse and killer immunoglobin-like receptor family in humans play a central role in NK cell immunity through recognition of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) and related molecules.
source: The Ly49 receptor family in the mouse and killer immunoglobin-like receptor family in humans play a central role in NK cell immunity through recognition of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) and related molecules.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about NK cell receptor families

claim: Mice lacking expression of all Ly49s were unable to reject missing-self target cells in vivo.
source: Herein, we showed mice lacking expression of all Ly49s were unable to reject missing-self target cells in vivo, were defective in NK cell licensing, and displayed lower KLRG1 on the surface of NK cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in vivo cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 2C

claim: Mice lacking expression of all Ly49s were defective in NK cell licensing.
source: Herein, we showed mice lacking expression of all Ly49s were unable to reject missing-self target cells in vivo, were defective in NK cell licensing, and displayed lower KLRG1 on the surface of NK cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from anti-NK1.1 stimulation assays shown in Figure 2A

claim: Mice lacking expression of all Ly49s displayed lower KLRG1 on the surface of NK cells.
source: Herein, we showed mice lacking expression of all Ly49s were unable to reject missing-self target cells in vivo, were defective in NK cell licensing, and displayed lower KLRG1 on the surface of NK cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored missing-self target cell rejection.
source: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored missing-self target cell rejection, NK cell licensing, and NK cell KLRG1 expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in vivo cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 4C

claim: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored NK cell licensing.
source: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored missing-self target cell rejection, NK cell licensing, and NK cell KLRG1 expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from anti-NK1.1 stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored NK cell KLRG1 expression.
source: Expression of Ly49A alone on an H-2Dd background restored missing-self target cell rejection, NK cell licensing, and NK cell KLRG1 expression.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A single inhibitory Ly49 receptor is sufficient to license NK cells and mediate missing-self in vivo.
source: Thus, a single inhibitory Ly49 receptor is sufficient to license NK cells and mediate missing-self in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figures 3 and 4 showing rescue of licensing and missing-self rejection by Ly49A alone

claim: NK cells can mediate effective immunity against viruses and cancer through direct lysis and cytokine production.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) that can mediate effective immunity against viruses and cancer through direct lysis and cytokine production (Huntington et al., 2020; Piersma and Brizić, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: NK cells recognize their target cells through integration of signals by germline-encoded activation and inhibitory receptors.
source: NK cells recognize their target cells through integration of signals by germline-encoded activation and inhibitory receptors (Long et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Inhibitory receptors include members of the Ly49 family in the mouse that are encoded by the Klra gene family.
source: These inhibitory receptors include members of the Ly49 family in the mouse that are encoded by the Klra gene family and killer immunoglobin-like receptor (KIR) family in humans and they prevent killing of healthy cells through recognition of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) (Colonna and Samaridis, 1995; Karlhofer et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Inhibitory receptors prevent killing of healthy cells through recognition of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I).
source: These inhibitory receptors include members of the Ly49 family in the mouse that are encoded by the Klra gene family and killer immunoglobin-like receptor (KIR) family in humans and they prevent killing of healthy cells through recognition of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) (Colonna and Samaridis, 1995; Karlhofer et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Host cells may lose surface MHC-I expression in response to virus infection or malignant transformation.
source: Host cells may lose surface MHC-I expression in response to virus infection or malignant transformation.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about viral immune evasion and cancer

claim: Cells that lose MHC-I expression become invisible to CD8+ T cells.
source: As a result, these cells become invisible to CD8+ T cells, but simultaneously become targets for NK cells through 'missing-self' recognition (Kärre et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on missing-self recognition

claim: Cells that lose MHC-I expression become targets for NK cells through 'missing-self' recognition.
source: As a result, these cells become invisible to CD8+ T cells, but simultaneously become targets for NK cells through 'missing-self' recognition (Kärre et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on missing-self recognition

claim: The inhibitory Ly49 molecules appear to be responsible for missing-self recognition in mice.
source: The inhibitory Ly49 molecules appear to be responsible for missing-self recognition in mice (Babić et al., 2010; Bélanger et al., 2012; Gamache et al., 2019; Parikh et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The Ly49 family is highly polymorphic and differs between mouse strains.
source: However, it has been sometimes challenging to draw definitive conclusions because the Ly49 family is highly polymorphic and differs between mouse strains.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about Ly49 receptor diversity

claim: Multiple inhibitory Ly49 receptors within a single host can recognize a given MHC-I molecule.
source: Moreover, multiple inhibitory Ly49 receptors within a single host can recognize a given MHC-I molecule while others apparently have no ligands and instead recognize other MHC-I alleles (Schenkel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In the C57BL/6 background, Ly49C and Ly49I can recognize H-2b MHC-I molecules that include H-2Kb and H-2Db.
source: For example, in the C57BL/6 background, Ly49C and Ly49I can recognize H-2b MHC-I molecules that include H-2Kb and H-2Db, while Ly49A and Ly49G cannot recognize H-2b molecules and instead they recognize H-2d alleles.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about Ly49 receptor specificities

claim: Ly49A and Ly49G cannot recognize H-2b molecules and instead they recognize H-2d alleles.
source: For example, in the C57BL/6 background, Ly49C and Ly49I can recognize H-2b MHC-I molecules that include H-2Kb and H-2Db, while Ly49A and Ly49G cannot recognize H-2b molecules and instead they recognize H-2d alleles.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about Ly49 receptor specificities

claim: Ly49A has been implicated in recognition of the non-classical MHC-I molecule H2-M3, which is upregulated in response to exposure to N-formylated peptides.
source: Ly49A has also been implicated in recognition of the non-classical MHC-I molecule H2-M3, which is upregulated in response to exposure to N-formylated peptides (Andrews et al., 2012; Chiu et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The binding of Ly49A to H-2Dd has been confirmed by crystallographic studies.
source: For example, the binding of Ly49A to H-2Dd has been confirmed by crystallographic studies (Tormo et al., 1999), and validated by mutational analysis of both Ly49A and H-2Dd (Matsumoto et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published crystallographic and mutational studies

claim: The binding of Ly49A to H-2Dd has been validated by mutational analysis of both Ly49A and H-2Dd.
source: For example, the binding of Ly49A to H-2Dd has been confirmed by crystallographic studies (Tormo et al., 1999), and validated by mutational analysis of both Ly49A and H-2Dd (Matsumoto et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mutational studies

claim: The MHC-I specificities of other Ly49s have been primarily studied with MHC tetramers containing human β2-microglobulin (B2m), which is not recognized by Ly49A.
source: By contrast, the MHC-I specificities of other Ly49s have been primarily studied with MHC tetramers containing human β2-microglobulin (B2m), which is not recognized by Ly49A (Mitsuki et al., 2004), on cells overexpressing Ly49s (Hanke et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Ly49 receptors that recognize their cognate MHC-I ligands are involved in the licensing or education of NK cells to acquire functional competence.
source: In addition to effector function in missing-self, Ly49 receptors that recognize their cognate MHC-I ligands are involved in the licensing or education of NK cells to acquire functional competence.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about NK cell licensing

claim: NK cell licensing is characterized by potent effector functions including IFNγ production and degranulation in response to activation receptor stimulation.
source: NK cell licensing is characterized by potent effector functions including IFNγ production and degranulation in response to activation receptor stimulation (Elliott et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Inhibitory Ly49s require SHP-1 for NK cell licensing, which interacts with the ITIM-motif encoded in the cytosolic tail of inhibitory Ly49s.
source: Like missing-self recognition, inhibitory Ly49s require SHP-1 for NK cell licensing, which interacts with the ITIM-motif encoded in the cytosolic tail of inhibitory Ly49s (Bern et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2005; Viant et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Lower expression of SHP-1, particularly within the immunological synapse, is associated with licensed NK cells.
source: Moreover, lower expression of SHP-1, particularly within the immunological synapse, is associated with licensed NK cells (Schmied et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The Makrigiannis group targeted the promotor of Klra15 encoding Ly49O in 129 ES cells and resulting mice were subsequently backcrossed to C57BL/6 background.
source: This was pioneered by the Makrigiannis group, which targeted the promotor of Klra15 encoding Ly49O in 129 ES cells and resulting mice were subsequently backcrossed to C57BL/6 background (Bélanger et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mice with targeted Klra15 promotor were defective in the rejection of MHC-I-deficient target cells in vivo and exhibited reduced tumor control.
source: These mice were defective in the rejection of MHC-I-deficient target cells in vivo and exhibited reduced tumor control as well (Tu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mice with targeted Klra15 promotor had limited surface expression of NKG2A as well as Ly49s.
source: However, there was limited surface expression of NKG2A as well as Ly49s so these target defects were not solely dependent on the absence of Ly49s.
evidence: Inferred from the description of the phenotype of these mice

claim: The Dong group deleted the entire 1.4 Mb Klra locus in the C57BL/6 NKC and showed that Ly49-deficient mice were unable to reject MHC-I-deficient cells in vivo at steady state.
source: Following the development of mouse CRISPR engineering, the Dong group deleted the entire 1.4 Mb Klra locus in the C57BL/6 NKC and showed that Ly49-deficient mice were unable to reject MHC-I-deficient cells in vivo at steady state (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In mice with the entire Klra locus deleted, surface expression of KLRG1, NKG2A, NKG2D, and CD94 was reduced.
source: Besides loss of Ly49 receptor expression, surface expression of other receptors, including KLRG1, NKG2A, NKG2D, and CD94, was also reduced in these mice.
evidence: Inferred from the description of the phenotype of these mice

claim: ΔLy49-1 mice contain a 66 kb and 149 kb deletion in the C57BL/6 Klra locus, resulting in the loss of four Ly49 molecules, including Ly49A and Ly49G.
source: Around the same time, we generated a mouse that contains a 66 kb and 149 kb deletion in the C57BL/6 Klra locus, resulting in the loss of four Ly49 molecules, including Ly49A and Ly49G (Parikh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: ΔLy49-1 mice were deficient in H2Dd-restricted control of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV).
source: The resulting ΔLy49-1 mice were also deficient in H2Dd-restricted control of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), which was rescued by knock-in of Ly49A into the Ncr1 locus.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The MCMV control deficiency in ΔLy49-1 mice was rescued by knock-in of Ly49A into the Ncr1 locus.
source: The resulting ΔLy49-1 mice were also deficient in H2Dd-restricted control of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), which was rescued by knock-in of Ly49A into the Ncr1 locus.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Individual Ly49s are stochastically expressed on NK cells.
source: The current data, however, do not take into account that individual Ly49s are stochastically expressed on NK cells, and multiple receptors are simultaneously expressed on individual NK cells, resulting in a diverse Ly49 repertoire of potential specificities on overlapping subsets of NK cells (Dorfman and Raulet, 1998; Kubota et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Multiple receptors are simultaneously expressed on individual NK cells, resulting in a diverse Ly49 repertoire of potential specificities on overlapping subsets of NK cells.
source: The current data, however, do not take into account that individual Ly49s are stochastically expressed on NK cells, and multiple receptors are simultaneously expressed on individual NK cells, resulting in a diverse Ly49 repertoire of potential specificities on overlapping subsets of NK cells (Dorfman and Raulet, 1998; Kubota et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Klra genes encoding the Ly49 receptor family are highly related and clustered together, resulting in a high concentration of repetitive elements.
source: However, Klra genes encoding the Ly49 receptor family are highly related and clustered together, resulting in a high concentration of repetitive elements (Makrigiannis et al., 2005), complicating the capacity to target individual Klra genes for definitive analysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In ΔLy49-1 mice, the percentage of NK cells expressing Ly49D was markedly reduced, even though Ly49D was otherwise expressed at normal levels.
source: Moreover, in ΔLy49-1 mice, which had an intact Klra4 coding sequence encoding Ly49D, the percentage of NK cells expressing Ly49D was markedly reduced, even though Ly49D was otherwise expressed at normal levels, suggesting a regulatory locus control region within the deleted fragments (Parikh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The reduced Ly49D expression in ΔLy49-1 mice suggests a regulatory locus control region within the deleted fragments.
source: Moreover, in ΔLy49-1 mice, which had an intact Klra4 coding sequence encoding Ly49D, the percentage of NK cells expressing Ly49D was markedly reduced, even though Ly49D was otherwise expressed at normal levels, suggesting a regulatory locus control region within the deleted fragments (Parikh et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced Ly49D expression despite intact coding sequence

claim: The Ly49KO mouse contains a fusion between Klra9 and Klra17 with a deletion of the start codon and insertion of a fusion sequence that contains a potential start site for a putative five amino acid polypeptide.
source: The resulting mouse contained a fusion between Klra9 and Klra17 with a deletion of the start codon and insertion of a fusion sequence that did contain a potential start site for a putative five amino acid polypeptide (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis and sequencing data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The 3′ deletion in the ΔLy49-1 mouse results in a frameshift and a premature stop codon after nine amino acids in the fused Klra7/1 gene.
source: We confirmed that the 3′ deletion reported in the ΔLy49-1 mouse was unaffected, resulting in a frameshift and a premature stop codon after nine amino acids in the fused Klra7/1 gene.
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis and sequencing data

claim: Genetic and sequencing analysis revealed all Ly49 genes were disrupted in the Ly49KO mouse.
source: Thus, genetic and sequencing analysis revealed all Ly49 genes were disrupted and we termed this mouse line Ly49KO (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis and sequencing data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed loss of cell surface expression of Ly49 molecules in homozygous Ly49KO mice.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed loss of cell surface expression of Ly49 molecules in homozygous Ly49KO mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: NKG2A, CD94, and NKG2D molecules that are encoded by the NKG2 locus were still expressed in Ly49KO mice, albeit at marginally lower frequencies.
source: NKG2A, CD94, and NKG2D molecules that are encoded by the NKG2 locus, located next to the Ly49 locus, were still expressed, albeit at marginally lower frequencies (Figure 1C; Yokoyama and Plougastel, 2003).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and citation to published literature

claim: 2B4 and CD122 expression were unaffected in Ly49KO mice.
source: Unrelated molecules 2B4 and CD122 were unaffected.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In heterozygous Ly49KO mice, the percentages of NK cells expressing Ly49A, Ly49C, Ly49D, Ly49G2, Ly49H, and Ly49I were reduced by 33–41%.
source: In heterozygous Ly49KO mice, the percentages of NK cells expressing Ly49A, Ly49C, Ly49D, Ly49G2, Ly49H, and Ly49I were reduced by 33–41%.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The median fluorescent intensity (MFI) for Ly49I was reduced by 26% in Ly49I+ NK cells in heterozygous Ly49KO mice.
source: The median fluorescent intensity (MFI) for Ly49I was reduced by 26% in Ly49I+ NK cells in heterozygous Ly49KO mice, while the other Ly49s did not display significant differences in MFI.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Ly49KO NK cells showed a 51% reduction in KLRG1 expression.
source: Consistent with apparent dependence of normal KLRG1 expression on MHC-I expression (Corral et al., 2000) and previous reports (Zhang et al., 2019), Ly49KO NK cells showed a 51% reduction in KLRG1 expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and citations to published literature

claim: NK cells in Ly49KO mice displayed similar maturation to wildtype NK cells, based on the expression of the surface markers CD27 and CD11b.
source: NK cells in Ly49KO mice displayed similar maturation to wildtype NK cells, based on the expression of the surface markers CD27 and CD11b (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Stimulation of Ly49KO NK cells with anti-NK1.1 resulted in a 73% reduction in IFNγ production compared to wildtype NK cells.
source: Stimulation of Ly49KO NK cells with anti-NK1.1 resulted in a 73% reduction in IFNγ production compared to wildtype NK cells, similar to unlicensed NK cells from H-2Kb and H-2Db double-deficient (KODO) mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 2A

claim: Both Ly49KO and KODO NK cells produced high amounts of IFNγ in response to phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) plus ionomycin.
source: Both Ly49KO and KODO NK cells produced high amounts of IFNγ in response to phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) plus ionomycin (Figure 2B), indicating that their IFNγ production machinery is intact.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 2B

claim: The IFNγ production machinery is intact in Ly49KO and KODO NK cells.
source: Both Ly49KO and KODO NK cells produced high amounts of IFNγ in response to phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) plus ionomycin (Figure 2B), indicating that their IFNγ production machinery is intact.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that these cells produce IFNγ in response to PMA/ionomycin

claim: Wildtype mice efficiently rejected MHC-I KO and H-2Kb KO target cells.
source: While wildtype mice efficiently rejected MHC-I KO and H-2Kb KO target cells, only 13% of H-2Db KO target cells were rejected by wildtype mice, indicating that missing-self recognition in the C57BL/6 background depends on the absence of H-2Kb rather than H-2Db.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Only 13% of H-2Db KO target cells were rejected by wildtype mice.
source: While wildtype mice efficiently rejected MHC-I KO and H-2Kb KO target cells, only 13% of H-2Db KO target cells were rejected by wildtype mice, indicating that missing-self recognition in the C57BL/6 background depends on the absence of H-2Kb rather than H-2Db.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Missing-self recognition in the C57BL/6 background depends on the absence of H-2Kb rather than H-2Db.
source: While wildtype mice efficiently rejected MHC-I KO and H-2Kb KO target cells, only 13% of H-2Db KO target cells were rejected by wildtype mice, indicating that missing-self recognition in the C57BL/6 background depends on the absence of H-2Kb rather than H-2Db.
evidence: Inferred from the differential rejection of H-2Kb KO versus H-2Db KO target cells

claim: None of the target cell populations were rejected in the Ly49KO mice.
source: None of the target cell populations were rejected in the Ly49KO mice, comparable to wildtype controls depleted of NK cells.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Ly49 molecules mediate NK cell-dependent MHC-I-deficient target cell killing in vivo under steady-state conditions.
source: Thus, Ly49 molecules mediate NK cell-dependent MHC-I-deficient target cell killing in vivo under steady-state conditions and rejection of MHC-I-deficient target cells is predominantly controlled by H-2Kb in the H-2b background.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Rejection of MHC-I-deficient target cells is predominantly controlled by H-2Kb in the H-2b background.
source: Thus, Ly49 molecules mediate NK cell-dependent MHC-I-deficient target cell killing in vivo under steady-state conditions and rejection of MHC-I-deficient target cells is predominantly controlled by H-2Kb in the H-2b background.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Ly49A expression in Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice closely follows NKp46 expression.
source: Ly49A expression in the resulting Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice closely follows NKp46 expression because NKp46- NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow of these mice do not express Ly49A, while virtually all the NKp46+ NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow and spleen express Ly49A (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: NKp46- NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow of Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice do not express Ly49A.
source: Ly49A expression in the resulting Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice closely follows NKp46 expression because NKp46- NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow of these mice do not express Ly49A, while virtually all the NKp46+ NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow and spleen express Ly49A (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Virtually all the NKp46+ NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow and spleen of Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice express Ly49A.
source: Ly49A expression in the resulting Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice closely follows NKp46 expression because NKp46- NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow of these mice do not express Ly49A, while virtually all the NKp46+ NK1.1+ NK cells in the bone marrow and spleen express Ly49A (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO NK cells expressed robust levels of Ly49A, albeit at lower MFI compared to Ly49A expression on D8-KODO NK cells.
source: Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO NK cells expressed robust levels of Ly49A, albeit at lower MFI compared to Ly49A expression on D8-KODO NK cells, consistent with prior observations with wildtype Ly49A and H2Dd (Held et al., 1996; Karlhofer et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and citations to published literature

claim: NK cells were able to fully mature in Ly49KO D8-KODO and Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice as observed by similar percentage of mature CD27- CD11b+ NK cells in the spleen, bone marrow, and liver.
source: NK cells were able to fully mature in Ly49KO D8-KODO and Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice as we observed similar percentage of mature CD27- CD11b+ NK cells in the spleen, bone marrow, and liver (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was a modest significant increase in immature CD27+ CD11b- NK cells in the bone marrow of Ly49KO D8-KODO and Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice.
source: While there was a modest significant increase in immature CD27+ CD11b- NK cells in the bone marrow of Ly49KO D8-KODO and Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice, no differences were observed in NK cell maturation in the spleen and liver.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The decrease in the frequency of KLRG1+ NK cells observed in the Ly49KO NK cells on the H-2b background was recapitulated in the D8-KODO background.
source: The decrease in the frequency of KLRG1+ NK cells observed in the Ly49KO NK cells on the H-2b background was recapitulated in the D8-KODO background (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Expression of Ly49A in Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice rescued KLRG1 expression and resulted in similar levels of KLRG1 as D8-KODO NK cells.
source: Intriguingly, expression of Ly49A in Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO mice rescued KLRG1 expression and resulted in similar levels of KLRG1 as D8-KODO NK cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C

claim: In D8-KODO mice, Ly49A+ NK cells displayed increased levels of IFNγ production and degranulation measured by CD107 in response to plate-bound anti-NK1.1 stimulation compared to all NK cells including unlicensed cells.
source: In D8-KODO mice, Ly49A+ NK cells displayed increased levels of IFNγ production and degranulation measured by CD107 in response to plate-bound anti-NK1.1 stimulation compared to all NK cells including unlicensed cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: Ly49KO NK cells on the D8-KODO background showed a 72% decrease in IFNγ production compared to Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
source: Similar to Ly49KO NK cells on the H-2b background, Ly49KO NK cells on the D8-KODO background showed a 72% decrease in IFNγ production, but also showed a 59% decrease in degranulation compared to Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: Ly49KO NK cells on the D8-KODO background showed a 59% decrease in degranulation compared to Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
source: Similar to Ly49KO NK cells on the H-2b background, Ly49KO NK cells on the D8-KODO background showed a 72% decrease in IFNγ production, but also showed a 59% decrease in degranulation compared to Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: The impaired IFNγ production and degranulation in Ly49KO NK cells was reversed in Ly49A KI NK cells on the Ly49KO D8-KODO background.
source: This impaired IFNγ production and degranulation was reversed in Ly49A KI NK cells on the Ly49KO D8-KODO background that showed similar IFNγ production and degranulation to Ly49A+ NK cells on the D8-KODO background, indicating that Ly49A KI NK cells are licensed.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: Ly49A KI NK cells on the Ly49KO D8-KODO background are licensed.
source: This impaired IFNγ production and degranulation was reversed in Ly49A KI NK cells on the Ly49KO D8-KODO background that showed similar IFNγ production and degranulation to Ly49A+ NK cells on the D8-KODO background, indicating that Ly49A KI NK cells are licensed.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ly49A KI NK cells show similar functional responses to licensed Ly49A+ NK cells

claim: There were no differences among all NK cell populations in IFNγ production and degranulation in response to PMA/Ionomycin.
source: Importantly, there were no differences among all NK cell populations in IFNγ production and degranulation in response to PMA/Ionomycin (Figure 4B), indicating that the IFNγ production and degranulation machinery are not affected in any of the mouse strains.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4B

claim: The IFNγ production and degranulation machinery are not affected in any of the mouse strains.
source: Importantly, there were no differences among all NK cell populations in IFNγ production and degranulation in response to PMA/Ionomycin (Figure 4B), indicating that the IFNγ production and degranulation machinery are not affected in any of the mouse strains.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all NK cell populations respond similarly to PMA/Ionomycin

claim: The Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO NK cells displayed a fully licensed phenotype comparable to licensed Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
source: Thus, the Ly49KO/Ly49A KI D8-KODO NK cells displayed a fully licensed phenotype comparable to licensed Ly49A+ NK cells in D8-KODO mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from in vitro stimulation assays shown in Figure 4A

claim: D8-KODO mice efficiently rejected KODO target splenocytes.
source: D8-KODO mice efficiently rejected KODO target splenocytes, while Ly49KO D8-KODO mice were unable to reject these cells.
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Ly49KO D8-KODO mice were unable to reject KODO target splenocytes.
